While the challenges of parenthood are well-documented, many people find that having children profoundly enhances their quality of life in ways that are emotional, psychological, and social.

Here are the various ways having children can improve a person's quality of life:

### 1. Emotional Fulfillment and Purpose
For many, children provide a powerful sense of meaning and direction.
*   **Unconditional Love:** The bond between a parent and child is often described as one of the most intense and selfless forms of love. Experiencing this can provide a deep sense of emotional security and belonging.
*   **A Sense of Legacy:** Raising children allows parents to pass down their values, traditions, and knowledge, creating a feeling of continuity and contribution to the future.
*   **Motivation for Self-Improvement:** Many parents find they are motivated to be better versions of themselves—more patient, hardworking, or empathetic—because they want to provide a positive role model for their children.

### 2. Psychological Growth and Personal Development
The demands of parenthood often act as a catalyst for personal growth.
*   **Developing Empathy and Patience:** Learning to navigate a child's needs and emotions often expands a parent's capacity for empathy and tolerance.
*   **Resilience and Problem-Solving:** Managing the unpredictability of children requires adaptability and creativity, which can translate into greater confidence and resilience in other areas of life.
*   **Rediscovering Wonder:** Seeing the world through a child's eyes allows adults to rediscover the joy in simple things—like

This lack of test opportunities led to a now common path of talented New Zealanders moving off shore for the chance to play test cricket- most notably in the pre WWII period of Clarrie Grimmet, who took over 200 test wickets playing for Australia. Since then, Andrew Caddick (234 test wickets at an average of 29.91) and Ben Stokes (5000+ test runs and 196 test wickets) have played leading roles for England in tests. If however we define the question as "the best test cricket player to have played for New Zealand", then there are perhaps only 3 or 4 candidates that feature. Of the current generation, there is no doubt that Kane Williamson will one day be regarded as the greatest player to have come from New Zealand- with over 8000 test runs at an average north of 50. With many years in front of him, Williamson will no doubt hold the crown of best test cricketer in years to come. Martin Crowe must likewise be regarded in the pantheon of test greats to have played for New Zealand- despite a slow start to his career, and injuries curtailing his time in the team, he amassed over 5000 runs at an average of over 45. However, most will agree that the most influential cricketer ever to play test cricket for New Zealand was Sir Richard Hadlee- the first cricketer to be knighted whilst still playing cricket for his country. Hadlee's bowling average of 22.29 is one of best in test cricket history, and at the time of his retirement he held the record for test wickets, at 431. Gaining 5 wickets in an innings 36 times was also a record, and led New Zealand to some of it's most famous test victories, notably victory in a series in Australia for the first time in 1985/86, with his best test figures of 15 for 123 coming in the first test at the Gabba. The appeal of coffee is a complex blend of biology, psychology, and social culture. People enjoy it for a variety of reasons, which can be broken down into four main categories:

### 1. Biological and Chemical Effects (The "Buzz")
The most immediate reason people drink coffee is for the **caffeine**, a natural stimulant.
*   **Adenosine Blockage:** Throughout the day, your brain builds up a molecule called adenosine, which tells your body it's time to sleep. Caffeine mimics the shape of adenosine and plugs into its receptors, effectively "blocking" the signal for sleepiness.
*   **Dopamine Release:** Caffeine triggers the release of dopamine and norepinephrine, which improves mood, increases alertness, and creates a feeling of mild euphoria.
*   **The Habit Loop:** Because caffeine creates a noticeable change in state (from tired to awake), the brain creates a reward loop, leading to a psychological craving for that "lift."

### 2. Sensory Pleasure (Taste and Smell)
Beyond the caffeine, many people are genuinely attracted to the sensory experience of coffee.
*   **Complexity of Flavor:** Coffee is one of the most chemically complex beverages in the world. Depending on the bean and roast, it can taste like chocolate, citrus, berries, or nuts.
*   **The Aroma:** The smell of brewing coffee is often cited as one of the most comforting scents. Olfactory nerves are linked directly to the brain's emotional center, meaning the smell of coffee can trigger feelings of comfort and coziness.

Primary factors include head size, length, weight, stiffness, and swingweight Head size - Power is closely correlated to head size - the larger the head size, the more power can be generated, all other factors being equal. A larger head size also provides larger hitting area and 'sweetspot'. Smaller head sizes tend to equate to more control and maneuverability. Length - The standard length is a 27 inches, but can range from 26.5 inches to 29 inches. A longer racquets provides more reach and often results in more power. Similar to head size, longer racquets may limit maneuverability and control. Weight - The heavier the racquet, the more power you will generate (increasing the 'swingweight') of the racquet. The lighter the racquet, the more maneuverable and easier it will be for players to get the racket to the right swing position. The balance of the racquet is also critical as part of weight. A more head light racket (more weight in the handle) provides increased maneuverability, especially when using a heavier racquet. A more balanced or head heavy racket are often reserved for lighter racquets to maintain the mass behind the ball Stiffness - Generally speaking, the stiffer the racket, the less energy is lost as the ball is redirected with your racquet and thus, creating more power. There is no single "best" surface for everyone; the right choice depends on your goals (speed vs. recovery), your injury history, and your current fitness level.

Here is a breakdown of the most common running surfaces, ranked from softest to hardest.

---

### 1. Synthetic Tracks (The Gold Standard for Speed)
Rubberized tracks are engineered to provide a balance of **shock absorption** (to protect joints) and **energy return** (to bounce you forward).
*   **Best for:** Speed work, intervals, and timed trials.
*   **Pros:** Extremely consistent, predictable, and reduces the risk of ankle sprains.
*   **Cons:** Running in circles for too long can put repetitive stress on one side of your body; they are not always accessible.

### 2. Dirt Trails and Natural Paths (The Best for Longevity)
Soft earth, pine needles, or packed dirt are generally the kindest surfaces for your joints.
*   **Best for:** Long runs, recovery runs, and overall joint health.
*   **Pros:** Very low impact. The uneven terrain strengthens the stabilizer muscles in your ankles and core.
*   **Cons:** Higher risk of tripping or twisting an ankle; can become muddy and slippery.

### 3. Grass (The Lowest Impact)
Grass is the softest natural surface, making it excellent for those recovering from an injury.
*   **Best for:** Recovery days or "easy" aerobic runs.
*   **Pros:** Maximum shock absorption.

The practice of switching between "winter" and "summer" clocks—officially known as **Daylight Saving Time (DST)**—was designed with one primary goal: **to make better use of natural sunlight.**

Here is the detailed breakdown of why we do it and how it works.

### 1. The Core Idea: "Shifting" the Light
The sun doesn’t rise and set at the same time year-round. In the summer, the days are longer. However, because our clocks are fixed, the sun often rises very early (sometimes at 4:00 or 5:00 AM), while most people are still asleep.

By moving the clocks forward one hour in the spring, we effectively "steal" an hour of light from the early morning (when nobody is using it) and move it to the evening. This means the sun sets later, giving people more daylight after they finish work or school.

### 2. The Primary Benefits
Historically, the shift to summer time was implemented for several reasons:

*   **Energy Saving:** This was the original driver during World War I and World War II. If it stays light later into the evening, people don't need to turn on their electric lights as early, reducing the demand for electricity.
*   **Economic Boost:** When people have more daylight after work, they are more likely to go shopping, eat at restaurants, or participate in outdoor recreation, which boosts the economy.
*   **Health and Safety:** More evening light is linked to increased physical

Sound travels fastest in **solids**, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases.

Here is the detailed explanation of why this happens.

### The Short Answer
Sound travels faster in solids because the molecules are packed much more closely together than in liquids or gases. This allows the vibration (the sound wave) to be passed from one particle to the next much more quickly.

---

### The Detailed "Why"

To understand why the medium matters, you have to look at what sound actually is: **a mechanical wave of pressure.** Sound is not a "thing" that moves through space; it is a vibration that travels through a substance.

#### 1. Molecular Density and Proximity
Sound travels by particles bumping into one another.

Determining the "most influential" president in history depends entirely on how you define influence. Influence can be measured by the expansion of government power, the preservation of the nation, the shaping of the global order, or the creation of long-lasting legal precedents.

Because of this, historians generally debate between a few key figures, depending on the criteria used:

### 1. George Washington (The Architect)
Washington is often cited as the most influential because he established the **precedents** for the office. 
*   **The Peaceful Transfer of Power:** By voluntarily stepping down after two terms, he ensured the U.S. would be a republic rather than a monarchy.
*   **Executive Authority:** He defined the role of the president in a way that the Constitution (which was intentionally vague) did not, setting the stage for every president who followed.

### 2. Abraham Lincoln (The Preserver)
Lincoln is frequently ranked as the greatest or most influential due to the existential stakes of his presidency.
*   **Preservation of the Union:** He navigated the Civil War, ensuring that the United States remained a single entity rather than splitting into two or more smaller nations.
*   **Ending Slavery:** Through the Emancipation Proclamation and his push for the 13th Amendment, he fundamentally altered the social and legal fabric of American society.

### 3. Franklin D. Roosevelt (The Transformer)
FDR is often seen as the most influential in terms of the **scope and power of the federal government.**

With a current seating capacity of 99,354, it is the largest stadium in Spain and Europe, and the second largest association football stadium in the world. It has hosted two European Cup/Champions League finals in 1989 and 1999, two European Cup Winners' Cup finals, four Inter-Cities Fairs Cup final games, five UEFA Super Cup games, four Copa del Rey finals, two Copa de la Liga finals, and twenty-one Supercopa de España finals. Following the approval of the sponsorship agreement with Spotify by FC Barcelona's Extraordinary Assembly of Delegate Members on 3 April 2022, the stadium was officially renamed on 1 July 2022 as Spotify Camp Nou. Here are the different ways to stop your car from being stolen, categorized by the type of security they provide.

### 1. Physical Deterrents (Visible Barriers)
These are designed to intimidate a thief and make the physical act of stealing the car more difficult.
*   **Steering Wheel Locks:** (e.g., "The Club") These are highly visible and tell a thief they will have to spend extra time and noise cutting through metal to steer the car.
*   **Wheel Clamps (Boots):** While impractical for daily use, these are excellent for long-term parking (like at an airport) as they make the car impossible to tow or drive.
*   **Brake Pedal Locks:** These lock the brake pedal in place, preventing the thief from shifting the car out of "Park."

### 2. Electronic & Tech-Based Security
These focus on preventing the engine from starting or alerting you if the car is moved.
*   **Kill Switches:** A hidden switch installed in the wiring that cuts power to the fuel pump or ignition. Even if a thief has the key, the car won't start unless the hidden switch is toggled.
*   **OBD Port Locks:** Modern thieves use "plug-and-play" devices to bypass immobil

When driving an electric vehicle (EV) on a long trip, the "estimated range" shown on your dashboard is a variable number, not a fixed one. Several external and internal factors can cause your actual mileage to deviate from the EPA or manufacturer estimates.

Here are the primary things that impact your EV range during long trips:

### 1. Speed (The Biggest Factor)
Aerodynamic drag increases exponentially as you speed up. 
*   **The "Wall":** While EVs are incredibly efficient in city traffic (due to regenerative braking), they lose efficiency quickly at highway speeds. Driving at 80 mph consumes significantly more energy per mile than driving at 65 mph.
*   **Wind Resistance:** Driving into a strong headwind creates "artificial speed," meaning the car has to work harder to push through the air, draining the battery faster.

### 2. Temperature (Ambient & Cabin)
Batteries are chemical devices, and they hate extreme temperatures.
*   **Cold Weather:** In winter, batteries become less efficient at delivering power. Additionally, you lose energy to **cabin heating**, which is much more taxing on a battery than cooling. (Unless your car has a heat pump, which is more efficient).
*   **Extreme Heat:** While batteries prefer warmth, very high temperatures require the car to run powerful cooling systems to keep the battery from overheating, which consumes energy.

### 3. Vehicle Load (Weight)
The more mass the motor has to move, the more energy it requires.

Bears are found across several continents, primarily in the **Northern Hemisphere**, though one species is native to South America. Their habitats vary wildly depending on the species.

Here is a breakdown of where different types of bears live:

### 1. North America
*   **Brown Bears (and Grizzlies):** Found across Alaska, Western Canada, and parts of the Northwestern United States. They prefer forests, alpine meadows, and coastal areas.
*   **Black Bears:** Found throughout most of North America, from Mexico up into Canada. They are primarily forest-dwellers.
*   **Polar Bears:** Live in the **Arctic Circle**, specifically on the sea ice and coasts of Canada, Alaska, Russia, Greenland, and Norway.

### 2. Asia
*   **Giant Pandas:** Native exclusively to south-central **China**, living in high-altitude bamboo forests.
*   **Asiatic Black Bears:** Found throughout Southern Asia, from the Himalayas to Southeast Asia.
*   **Sloth Bears:** Found primarily in **India**, Sri Lanka, and Nepal, living in grasslands and tropical forests.

### 3. South America
*   **Spectacled Bears (Andean Bears):** The only bear species native to South America. They live in the **Andes Mountains** (Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Venezuela), ranging from cloud forests to high-altitude grasslands.

### 4. Europe and Russia
*   **Brown Bears:** Found across Europe (from Scandinavia to the Balkans) and throughout the vast forests

*   **Innovation:** It often pushes the boundaries of the English language or narrative structure to create a uniquely "American" voice.
*   **Cultural Impact:** It must transcend its time of publication and remain relevant to future generations.

There are three types of optical illusions: Physical, physiological and cognitive. Physical optical illusion occurs when the light bends or changes direction before it reaches human eye. When light travels through different mediums such as air , water or glass, its speed changes and change in speed causes the light to bend. This phenomenon is called refraction. Rainbow is an example of physical optical illusion caused by refraction. Physiological optical illusion occurs when a pattern repeats over and over again and it is too much information for the brain. This causes the brain to think the images are moving. Kinetoscope uses images to create a video using physiological optical illusion.

**Lemuel "Lem" Tucker** (1938–1991) was a pioneering American journalist and one of the first African Americans to serve as a television network reporter.

**Career Highlights:**
*   **Network Experience:** He worked for all three major U.S. networks: NBC (starting in 1965), ABC (joining in 1972), and CBS (joining in 1977), where he remained until his death.
*   **Major Assignments:** Tucker covered some of the most significant events of the 20th century, including the Vietnam War, the Iran hostage crisis, the Kent State shootings, the Woodstock Festival, and various civil unrests in cities like Newark, Miami, and Harlem.
*   **The Reagan Assassination Attempt:** In 1981, he was present at the Washington Hilton Hotel during the shooting of President Ronald Reagan and provided immediate, thorough live coverage for CBS Radio.
*   **Awards:** He won two Emmy Awards—one in 1979 for his coverage of black America and another in 1983 for a series on hunger in America.

**Education and Early Achievements:**
Tucker graduated from Central Michigan University (CMU) in 1960. He made history there as the first African American elected student body president at the university, a notable feat given that less than one percent of the student body was Black at the time. He was also a standout forensic student and president of the Pi Kappa Delta speech honorary fraternity

Based on the text provided, **Oxygen Not Included** is a survival simulation video game developed by Klei Entertainment. 

Here is a summary of the game's key elements:

**The Premise**
Players manage three colonists, known as "duplicants," who wake up on an asteroid with no memory of how they arrived. The goal is to keep these duplicants alive and build a sustainable space colony.

**Gameplay Mechanics**
*   **Resource Management:** Players must monitor essential needs, including hunger, waste, and oxygen levels.
*   **Exploration:** The game features procedurally generated worlds divided into "biomes." Players must prepare for hazards like vacuums, diseases, and extreme temperatures as they expand.
*   **Simulation:** The game realistically simulates the physics of gas diffusion, atmospheric equalization, and the effects of gravity on liquids.
*   **Indirect Control:** Players do not control duplicants directly. Instead, they provide prioritized instructions (such as mining, crafting, or researching), and the duplicants execute them based on their individual stats and skills.

**Core Activities**
To survive, the player directs their colony to:
*   Mine for resources and craft equipment.
*   Grow food and maintain hygiene and rest.
*   Research new technologies to improve the colony.

*   **The Government:** The remnants of the government exist only in isolated compounds, performing irrelevant "make-work."
*   **Institutional Shifts:** Traditional government agencies have evolved into for-profit entities, such as the CIC (a merger of the CIA and the Library of Congress).

Based on the definition provided, here is a summary of how to determine if a number is prime or composite:

### 1. Check the Basic Requirements
*   **Must be a natural number:** It must be a whole counting number (1, 2, 3...).
*   **Must be greater than 1:** By definition, the number 1 is neither prime nor composite.

### 2. Test for Factors
To determine if a number is prime, check if it can be created by multiplying two smaller natural numbers:
*   **If it is Prime:** The only way to write the number as a product is **1 × itself**. No other whole numbers divide into it evenly.
*   **If it is Composite:** There is at least one way to write the number as a product of two smaller numbers (e.g., $4 = 2 \times 2$).

| **Composite** | Divisible by numbers other than 1 and itself | **4** (divisible by $2 \times 2$) |
| **Neither** | The number 1 | **1** |

Susan Wise Bauer took inspiration from Mortimer Adler's book, "How to Read A Book", in writing her book, "The Well-Educated Mind, A Guide to the Classical Education You Never Had." One of the highlights of the book is a reading list of classics from six genres of writing. The six genres Bauer focuses upon are novels, autobiography, history and politics, drama, poetry and natural sciences. She describes how to approach each genre as a reader, how to ask good questions of the author and how to formulate your own viewpoint of the topic. For each genre, when presenting the book list, she gives you a summary of each book, the best revision of the book to read and her initial impressions of the authors viewpoint. Bauer's book is not meant to be read from cover to cover, but to be a guide as you work through the reading list of each genre. Reading Bauer's book is like having your own college level professor guiding you through the classics. At the end of this guide, if you have read every book on Bauer's recommended list, you will be able to consider yourself well read. **AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)** is a high-performance mode of operation for the AES symmetric-key cipher. It is classified as **Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)**, meaning it provides two critical security guarantees simultaneously:

1.  **Confidentiality:** It encrypts the data so that unauthorized parties cannot read it.
2.  **Authenticity/Integrity:** It ensures that the data has not been tampered with and originates from a trusted source.

A unique feature of GCM is its ability to handle **Associated Data (AD)**. This is information that needs to be authenticated (protected from tampering) but does not need to be kept secret (it remains unencrypted). This is commonly used for network packet headers.

**1. Review Frequency and Governance**
The index composition is reviewed **quarterly** by an independent **Index Steering Committee** (known in French as the *Conseil Scientifique*).

**2. Ranking Criteria**
All companies listed on Euronext Paris are ranked based on two specific metrics from the previous 12 months:
*   **Free float market capitalization**
*   **Share turnover**

**3. Selection Process**
*   **The Pool:** The committee starts with the **top 100 companies** from the ranking mentioned above.
*   **The Final Cut:** From those 100, **40 companies** are selected. 
*   **The Goal:** The selection is made to ensure the index remains a "relevant benchmark for portfolio management" and a "suitable underlying asset for derivatives products."

**4. Specific Rules**
*   **Share Classes:** If a company has multiple classes of shares, only the **most actively traded** class (usually the ordinary share) is admitted.
*   **Implementation:** Any changes resulting from the review are implemented at least **two weeks after** the meeting takes place.

Based on the text provided, here are the details about parity plots:

**Definition and Purpose**
*   **What it is:** A scatterplot used to compare results from a computational model against benchmark data.
*   **Purpose:** Used in scientific papers and reports to visually validate a model.

**Structure and Mechanics**
*   **Coordinates:** Each point consists of an **x** value (benchmark data) and a **y** value (model result).
*   **Reference Line:** A line representing the equation **y = x** is often added to show perfect model performance.
*   **Indication of Success:** When a point lies directly on the reference line, the model has successfully reproduced the benchmark.

**Limitations and Alternatives**
*   **Weakness:** When data has a wide range, the large scale can hide important discrepancies, making the model appear more accurate than it is.

Based on the text provided, the main core idea of the Transformer model can be summarized into these three key pillars:

**1. The Self-Attention Mechanism**
The defining feature of the Transformer is **self-attention**. This allows the model to differentially weight the importance of different parts of the input data. Instead of treating every word equally, it provides context for any position in the sequence, enabling the model to understand how different words relate to one another regardless of their distance from each other.

**2. Parallel Processing (Departure from RNNs)**
Unlike previous models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) or LSTMs—which process data sequentially (one word at a time)—Transformers **process the entire input all at once**. 

**3. Scalability and Efficiency**
Because they do not rely on sequential processing, Transformers allow for significantly more **parallelization**. This leads to two major advantages:
* **Reduced training times:** The model can be trained much faster.
* **Larger datasets:** The efficiency allows the models to be trained on massive datasets (like the Wikipedia Corpus), which paved the way for modern LLMs like BERT and GPT.

When light travels through different mediums such as air , water or glass, its speed changes and change in speed causes the light to bend. This phenomenon is called refraction. Rainbow is an example of physical optical illusion caused by refraction. Physiological optical illusion occurs when a pattern repeats over and over again and it is too much information for the brain. This causes the brain to think the images are moving. Kinetoscope uses images to create a video using physiological optical illusion. Flip books are another example of physiological optical illusion. Cognitive optical illusion occurs when multiple people view the same image but they interpret it differently. Interpretation of the image depends of people's past experience and personalities. The easiest way to understand aliasing is through a visual example you have likely already seen: **the "wagon-wheel effect" in movies or videos.**

### The Scenario
Imagine you are watching a video of a car driving down the street. You look at the wheels, and for a moment, it looks like the wheels are **spinning backward**, or perhaps they are standing perfectly still, even though you know the car is moving forward.

### Why this happens (The Layman's Explanation)
To understand why this happens, you have to understand how a camera works. A camera doesn't record "continuous" motion; it takes a series of still snapshots (samples) many times per second (the frame rate).

**Here is the breakdown of the "Aliasing" event:**

1.  **The Real Signal:** The wheel is spinning very fast (let's say it completes one full rotation every 1/40th of a second).
2.  **The Sampling:** Your camera is taking pictures at 30 frames per second.
3.  **The "Alias":** Because the wheel is spinning faster than the camera can "sample" it, the camera misses the majority of the rotation. 
    *   In Frame 1, the valve stem of the tire is at the top.
    *   By Frame 2, the wheel has spun almost all the way around, but not quite. To your eye, the valve stem now looks like it moved *backward* a little bit.

Based on the text provided, here is a comprehensive explanation of Marketing Automation:

### **Definition**
Marketing Automation is a specialized subset of **Customer Relationship Management (CRM)** or **Customer Experience Management (CXM)**. It involves using technology to automate repetitive, manual tasks within a marketing campaign to increase efficiency and enable new processes that were previously impossible.

### **How it Works**
Marketing Automation platforms act as a centralized tool that allows marketers to manage complex, **omnichannel strategies** from one place. These tools often integrate with or pull data from a CRM to better understand customer preferences and the overall impact of their campaigns.

### **Key Functions**
The technology focuses on four primary administrative areas:
1. **Definition:** Setting up the parameters of a campaign.
2. **Segmentation:** Dividing audiences into specific groups.
3. **Scheduling:** Determining when communications are sent.
4. **Tracking:** Monitoring the performance and results of the campaign.

### **Primary Use Cases**
Marketing Automation is particularly effective in the following areas of the customer journey:
*   **Lead Management:** Handling lead generation, nurturing, and lead scoring.
*   **Sales Growth:** Driving cross-selling and up-selling opportunities.
*   **Customer Loyalty:** Managing relationship marketing and customer retention.
*   **Analysis:** Measuring the Return on Investment (ROI) of marketing efforts.

Walt Disney passed away in December 1966 during the initial planning stages. While the company initially hesitated to move forward, Walt's brother, Roy O. Disney, returned from retirement to ensure the project was completed.

The complex expanded over several decades with the opening of four major parks:

For companies that are incorporated in Delaware, the Delaware General Corporation Law permits corporations to divide their boards of directors into up to 3 classes. Other states in the United States have similar provisions regarding classified boards. For boards that have only 1 class, each director serves a fixed term (generally 1 year), and each director is subject to re-election each year. Classified boards (also known as staggered boards) are divided into three separate classes (in equal proportion, to the extent possible), with members of each class serving three-year terms and only one class of directors up for election in any year. A classified board is one type of protection that companies consider as part of a wider range review of corporate defensive measures. Generally, corporate defensive measures relate to measures for a company to consider to protect against (1) hostile takeovers that the board believes do not reflect the value of the company and (2) short-termism, where there is pressure from public investors – particularly activist investors – to take board actions (or face the risk of being voted off the board) that the board believes are not in the best interest of the company and its stockholders and maximizing value over the long term. Corporate defensive measures generally aren’t relevant when a company is private given the corporate structure with significant long-term investor representation on the board and various agreements in place with stockholders. However, these measures become relevant once a company has public stockholders, so many companies who are considering an initial public offering will assess what types of defensive measures would be appropriate for them. A classified board is viewed as corporate defensive measure (i.e., it’s an anti-takeover and activist defense) as the entire board can’t be replaced in a single election cycle (with 3 classes, it would take up to the 3rd election cycle for the full board to be replaced, and generally 2 years to capture a majority). Based on the text provided, here is an explanation of what an **SVM (Support Vector Machine)** is:

### Core Definition
A Support Vector Machine is a **supervised learning model** used for both **classification** and **regression analysis**. At its most basic level, it is a non-probabilistic binary linear classifier.

### How it Works
1. **Mapping to Space:** The SVM takes training examples (which are already labeled into categories) and maps them as points in a multidimensional space.
2. **Maximizing the Gap:** The goal of the algorithm is to create a model that maximizes the **width of the gap** between the two different categories.
3. **Prediction:** When a new example is introduced, it is mapped into that same space. The SVM predicts which category the example belongs to based on which side of the gap it falls.

### Key Capabilities
*   **Linear Classification:** Dividing data into two distinct groups using a straight boundary.
*   **Non-Linear Classification (The "Kernel Trick"):** SVMs can handle complex, non-linear data by using a "kernel trick," which implicitly maps the input into high-dimensional feature spaces to find a way to separate the data.
*   **Unsupervised Learning:** While primarily supervised, the "support vector clustering" variation can be used to categorize unlabeled data by finding natural groupings (clusters).

### Origin
SVMs were developed at AT&T Bell Laboratories by Vladimir Vapnik and his colleagues, based on statistical learning frameworks known as **VC theory**.

There are three types of optical illusions: Physical, physiological and cognitive. Physical optical illusion occurs when the light bends or changes direction before it reaches human eye. When light travels through different mediums such as air , water or glass, its speed changes and change in speed causes the light to bend. This phenomenon is called refraction. Rainbow is an example of physical optical illusion caused by refraction. Physiological optical illusion occurs when a pattern repeats over and over again and it is too much information for the brain. This causes the brain to think the images are moving. Kinetoscope uses images to create a video using physiological optical illusion. Flip books are another example of physiological optical illusion. Cognitive optical illusion occurs when multiple people view the same image but they interpret it differently. Interpretation of the image depends of people's past experience and personalities. There are three common espresso machine designs for home use: manual, semi-automatic, and fully automatic. As the name implies -- manual machines require direct "manual" control by the user, who typically applies pressure through a lever to deliver the desired brew pressure. Semi-automatic machines require the user to prepare the coffee into the portafilter, but then rely on an automated pump and to deliver the desired brew pressure for espresso. Fully automatic machines automate the entire process end-to-end: grinding the beans, loading the ground beans into the portafilter, and then pumping water through the portafilter at predefined pressure levels to brew espresso. Manual machines typically have a lower cost, smaller footprint, and provide the user with more direct control over the brewing process. This allows skilled users to make higher-quality espresso than they would with a more automated machine. In contrast, fully automatic machines are often the easiest to use, but are unable to make espresso as consistently great as a skilled barista could with a manual machines. Fully automatic machines are inherently more complex, more expensive to purchase, and more likely to have longer-term reliability issues. Regardless of the type of espresso machine, two factors influence how well they will perform: their ability to manage brew temperature and brew pressure. A Chief Data Officer (CDO) is an executive responsible for managing a company's information as a strategic business asset. Their primary goal is to bridge the gap between technological capabilities and business outcomes.

Their responsibilities can be summarized into five key areas:

*   **Data Strategy & Utilization:** Determining what data to capture and exploit to drive revenue, reduce costs, and achieve digital transformation.
*   **Governance & Protection:** Establishing data ethics, protecting sensitive information, and eliminating "data territorialism" (silos) to ensure data is shared effectively across the enterprise.
*   **Operations & Usability:** Ensuring that data is available, efficient, and usable for the organization.
*   **Analytics & Insight:** Providing supporting reports and analytics regarding markets, customers, products, and operations to inform business decisions.
*   **Leadership:** Advising the executive team and monitoring enterprise data to align technical results with stakeholder values and customer needs.

**Key Distinction:** Unlike a Chief Digital Officer, who focuses on the *systems* used to store and process data, the CDO focuses on the *business value* and strategic use of the data itself.

A **Louisville Hot Brown** is an open-faced hot sandwich originating from the Brown Hotel in Louisville, Kentucky, where it was created by chef Fred K. Schmidt in 1926. It was designed as a hearty alternative to late-night ham and egg dinners.

**What it consists of:**
*   **The Base:** Sliced roast turkey and often ham on toasted white bread.
*   **The Sauce:** A creamy Mornay sauce (a Béchamel sauce with cheese, typically Cheddar or American).
*   **The Finish:** The sandwich is baked or broiled until the bread is crisp and the sauce is bubbly and brown.
*   **Garnishes:** It is traditionally topped with bacon strips and pimentos (though tomatoes or mushrooms are sometimes used).

The dish is a beloved local specialty in Kentucky and remains a signature item associated with the Brown Hotel.

An example of aliasing that easy to understand as a layman is the 'wagon wheel effect'. You've probably seen the wagon wheel effect when watching a movie or tv show and the wheels of a car appear to be spinning backwards even as the car moves forwards. This is an effect of aliasing. This occurs because the sampling rate of the film is not adequate to capture the frequency of the signal (the frequency that the tires are spinning forwards) and the signal becomes indistinguishable from another signal (a frequency of the tires spinning backwards). As an example of how this happens imagine that the camera's sampling rate allows it to record an image frame at about 90% of the frequency that the tires are spinning. That is, the tire is spinning fast enough that it rotates 90% around in between each picture the camera can take. In this case, the wheel will look like its rotated backwards by 10% of a rotation on each image. In climbing, "Free" is not the opposite of "Gear"; it is the opposite of **"Aid."**

### Free Climbing vs. Aid Climbing

To understand why climbers use gear during a "free" climb, you have to understand what **Aid Climbing** is:

*   **Aid Climbing:** The climber uses gear (bolts, nuts, cams) to physically pull themselves up. They might step on a piece of gear or pull on a strap to move to the next hold. In aid climbing, the gear is a **ladder**.
*   **Free Climbing:** The climber uses only their hands and feet on the natural features of the rock to move upward. The gear (ropes, harnesses, carabiners) is there **only to catch them if they fall**. In free climbing, the gear is a **safety net**.

### The Analogy: The Trapeze Artist
Think of a trapeze artist in a circus. They are performing a "free" aerial act. They are using their own strength and skill to swing and flip. However, there is a massive safety net underneath them. 

If the artist falls, the net catches them, but the net didn't help them perform the tricks. If the artist were to use a ladder to climb up to the trapeze, that would be "aid."

**The Setup**
* **The Field:** Played on a field with a 22-yard (20-metre) pitch at the center.
* **The Wicket:** Each end of the pitch has a wicket, which consists of three stumps with two bails balanced on top.

**The Objective**
* **The Batting Team:** Aims to score runs by hitting the ball bowled at the wicket and running between the wickets.
* **The Bowling/Fielding Team:** Aims to prevent runs and get the batters "out" (dismissed).

**How a Batter is Dismissed (Getting "Out")**
* **Bowled:** The ball hits the stumps and knocks off the bails.
* **Caught:** A fielder catches the ball after it is hit, before it touches the ground.
* **Run Out:** A fielder hits the wicket with the ball before the batter can cross the crease.

**Game Structure**
* **Innings:** An innings ends when ten batters have been dismissed, at which point the teams swap roles.
* **Formats:** The game varies in length, from **Twenty20** (20 overs per team, lasting about three hours) to **Test matches** (which can last up to five days).
* **Officiating:** The game is managed by two on-field

In business theory, disruptive innovation is innovation that creates a new market and value network or enters at the bottom of an existing market and eventually displaces established market-leading firms, products, and alliances. The concept was developed by the American academic Clayton Christensen and his collaborators beginning in 1995,[full citation needed] and has been called the most influential business idea of the early 21st century. Lingfei Wu, Dashun Wang, and James A. Evans generalized this term to identify disruptive science and technological advances from more than 65 million papers, patents and software products that span the period 1954–2014. Their work was featured as the cover of the February 2019 issue of Nature and was included among the Altmetric 100 most-discussed work in 2019. Not all innovations are disruptive, even if they are revolutionary. For example, the first automobiles in the late 19th century were not a disruptive innovation, because early automobiles were expensive luxury items that did not disrupt the market for horse-drawn vehicles. Morocco is unique as one of only three nations (including Spain and France) to have coastlines on both the **Atlantic Ocean** and the **Mediterranean Sea**.

    *   **The Rif Mountains:** Located in the north, stretching from the northwest to the northeast along the Mediterranean border.

There are three types of optical illusions: Physical, physiological and cognitive. Physical optical illusion occurs when the light bends or changes direction before it reaches human eye. When light travels through different mediums such as air , water or glass, its speed changes and change in speed causes the light to bend. This phenomenon is called refraction. Rainbow is an example of physical optical illusion caused by refraction. Physiological optical illusion occurs when a pattern repeats over and over again and it is too much information for the brain. This causes the brain to think the images are moving. Kinetoscope uses images to create a video using physiological optical illusion. Flip books are another example of physiological optical illusion. Cognitive optical illusion occurs when multiple people view the same image but they interpret it differently. Interpretation of the image depends of people's past experience and personalities. This occurs because the sampling rate of the film is not adequate to capture the frequency of the signal (the frequency that the tires are spinning forwards) and the signal becomes indistinguishable from another signal (a frequency of the tires spinning backwards). As an example of how this happens imagine that the camera's sampling rate allows it to record an image frame at about 90% of the frequency that the tires are spinning. Based on the provided text, **OLTP (Online Transaction Processing)** refers to information systems that facilitate and manage transaction-oriented applications.

Key characteristics of OLTP include:

*   **Purpose:** It is used to process transactions, which can refer to "atomic changes of state" in computer databases or "exchanges of economic entities" in business and finance. A common example is a bank's automated teller machine (ATM).
*   **Functionality:** These applications are insert- or update-intensive, processing a high volume of read, insert, update, and delete queries. They are designed to respond immediately to user requests and are often used concurrently by hundreds of users.
*   **Primary Goals:** The main objectives of OLTP are speed, availability, concurrency, and recoverability (durability).
*   **Business Benefits:** OLTP helps businesses by reducing paper trails and providing faster, more accurate forecasts for expenses and revenues.
*   **Contrasts:** 
    *   **Vs. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing):** While OLTP processes transactions, OLAP is used for business intelligence and reporting through complex, read-only queries.
    *   **Vs. OLEP (Online Event Processing):** OLTP is associated with short atomic transactions, whereas OLEP offers higher scalability and flexible distribution but with increased latency.

In business theory, disruptive innovation is innovation that creates a new market and value network or enters at the bottom of an existing market and eventually displaces established market-leading firms, products, and alliances. The concept was developed by the American academic Clayton Christensen and his collaborators beginning in 1995,[full citation needed] and has been called the most influential business idea of the early 21st century. Lingfei Wu, Dashun Wang, and James A. Evans generalized this term to identify disruptive science and technological advances from more than 65 million papers, patents and software products that span the period 1954–2014. Their work was featured as the cover of the February 2019 issue of Nature and was included among the Altmetric 100 most-discussed work in 2019. Not all innovations are disruptive, even if they are revolutionary. For example, the first automobiles in the late 19th century were not a disruptive innovation, because early automobiles were expensive luxury items that did not disrupt the market for horse-drawn vehicles. The market for transportation essentially remained intact until the debut of the lower-priced Ford Model T in 1908. The mass-produced automobile was a disruptive innovation, because it changed the transportation market, whereas the first thirty years of automobiles did not. Disruptive innovations tend to be produced by outsiders and entrepreneurs in startups, rather than existing market-leading companies. The business environment of market leaders does not allow them to pursue disruptive innovations when they first arise, because they are not profitable enough at first and because their development can take scarce resources away from sustaining innovations (which are needed to compete against current competition). Small teams are more likely to create disruptive innovations than large teams. A disruptive process can take longer to develop than by the conventional approach and the risk associated to it is higher than the other more incremental, architectural or evolutionary forms of innovations, but once it is deployed in the market, it achieves a much faster penetration and higher degree of impact on the established markets. Based on the text provided, the cost-effectiveness of the JDAM stems from the fact that it is not a standalone, purpose-built weapon, but rather a **"bolt-on" guidance package.**

Here is a breakdown of why this design makes it so cost-effective:

**1. Utilization of Existing Inventory**
Instead of manufacturing expensive, precision-guided missiles from scratch, the JDAM converts "dumb bombs" (unguided gravity bombs like the Mark 80 series) into precision munitions. This allows the military to use existing stockpiles of inexpensive, unguided bombs.

**2. Modular Design**
Because the JDAM is a kit consisting of a tail section, a strake kit, and a guidance unit, it can be attached to a variety of different bomb sizes (ranging from 500 to 2,000 pounds). This versatility means the military doesn't need a different expensive guidance system for every single bomb weight.

**3. Simplified Guidance Technology**
By using a combination of an inertial guidance system and GPS, the JDAM avoids the inherent limitations and potential costs associated with relying solely on laser-guided or infrared technology, which can be hindered by weather or ground conditions. This makes the weapon more reliable across more environments without requiring more expensive seeking hardware.

There are three common espresso machine designs for home use: manual, semi-automatic, and fully automatic. As the name implies -- manual machines require direct "manual" control by the user, who typically applies pressure through a lever to deliver the desired brew pressure. Semi-automatic machines require the user to prepare the coffee into the portafilter, but then rely on an automated pump and to deliver the desired brew pressure for espresso. Fully automatic machines automate the entire process end-to-end: grinding the beans, loading the ground beans into the portafilter, and then pumping water through the portafilter at predefined pressure levels to brew espresso. Manual machines typically have a lower cost, smaller footprint, and provide the user with more direct control over the brewing process. This allows skilled users to make higher-quality espresso than they would with a more automated machine. In contrast, fully automatic machines are often the easiest to use, but are unable to make espresso as consistently great as a skilled barista could with a manual machines. Fully automatic machines are inherently more complex, more expensive to purchase, and more likely to have longer-term reliability issues. Regardless of the type of espresso machine, two factors influence how well they will perform: their ability to manage brew temperature and brew pressure. **General Observances**
Holy Week is both a significant religious period and a major vacation. It is preceded by Lent, Carnival, a day dedicated to the Virgin of the Sorrows, and a Mass marking the disciples' abandonment of Jesus.

**Daily Traditions**
*   **Palm Sunday:** The week begins with the use of palms, which are often woven into intricate designs.
*   **Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Sunday:** These are the days when processions and Masses are most common.
*   **Good Friday:** Almost every community holds an event to mark the crucifixion of Jesus.
*   **Holy Saturday:** In the central and southern parts of the country, people participate in the "Burning of Judas."
*   **Easter Sunday:** The day is typically marked by the ringing of church bells and a Mass.

**Origins and Regionality**
While the traditions are primarily based on Spanish customs brought over during the conquest of the Aztec Empire, they have evolved with indigenous influences and colonial variations. Notable locations for these celebrations include San Luis Potosí, San Miguel de Allende, Taxco, and Iztapalapa in Mexico City.

**Michael Faraday** introduced the concept of the electric field.

**What it is:**
An electric field is a region of space created by a charged body that exerts a force on any other charges placed within it. It is a **vector field**, meaning it has both magnitude and direction. 

Key characteristics include:
*   **Behavior:** Like a gravitational field, it extends toward infinity and follows an inverse square relationship with distance.
*   **Attraction and Repulsion:** Unlike gravity (which only attracts), an electric field can either attract or repel charges.
*   **Measurement:** Its strength at any given point is defined as the force per unit charge that a stationary, negligible "test charge" would experience at that location.
*   **Visualization:** It can be visualized using "lines of force" (also introduced by Faraday) that originate at positive charges, terminate at negative charges, enter conductors at right angles, and never cross or close in on themselves.

There are three types of optical illusions: Physical, physiological and cognitive. Physical optical illusion occurs when the light bends or changes direction before it reaches human eye. When light travels through different mediums such as air , water or glass, its speed changes and change in speed causes the light to bend. This phenomenon is called refraction. Rainbow is an example of physical optical illusion caused by refraction. Physiological optical illusion occurs when a pattern repeats over and over again and it is too much information for the brain. This causes the brain to think the images are moving. Kinetoscope uses images to create a video using physiological optical illusion. Flip books are another example of physiological optical illusion. Cognitive optical illusion occurs when multiple people view the same image but they interpret it differently. Interpretation of the image depends of people's past experience and personalities. The **International Cricket Council (ICC)** is the global governing body for the sport of cricket. 

Key details about the organization include:

*   **Role:** It is responsible for the governance and organization of major international tournaments (such as the Cricket World Cup and T20 World Cup), appointing match officials (umpires and referees), and maintaining professional standards through its Code of Conduct.
*   **Integrity:** It coordinates efforts to fight match-fixing and corruption via its Anti-Corruption and Security Unit (ACSU).
*   **Membership:** It currently consists of 108 member nations, divided into 12 Full Members (who play Test matches) and 96 Associate Members.
*   **History:** Founded in 1909 as the Imperial Cricket Conference, it evolved into the International Cricket Conference in 1965 before adopting its current name in 1987.
*   **Location:** Its headquarters are located in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

E.E. Cummings is famous for his subversive approach to grammar and punctuation, and this poem is a masterclass in his philosophy. He utilizes "anti-syntax"—the intentional breaking of traditional linguistic rules—to mirror his thematic argument: that raw emotion is superior to intellectual structure. By eschewing capitalization and conventional punctuation, the poem feels fluid and spontaneous, mimicking the natural rush of passion rather than the rigid constraints of a textbook.

**Thematic Strength**
The poem is a powerful romantic manifesto. Its strength lies in its binary oppositions: **Feeling vs. Syntax**, **Foolishness vs. Wisdom**, and **Life vs. Paragraphs**. Cummings argues that the analytical mind (the "syntax of things") acts as a barrier to true intimacy. To "wholly kiss" someone requires a surrender of the ego and the intellect, a willingness to be a "fool."

**Imagery and Tone**
The tone is one of urgent, tender devotion. The imagery is grounded in the sensory and the organic—blood, flowers, and the "flutter" of eyelids. These are unpredictable, living things, contrasting with the "paragraphs" and "parentheses" of academic or structured thought.

**Who is Sasha?**
Sasha is not a separate person, but rather a **fake identity (an alter-ego)** created by the protagonist, Becky Green. Becky adopts the persona of Sasha to infiltrate a social circle of people who knew her estranged childhood friend, Chloe, in order to investigate the circumstances surrounding Chloe's suicide.

**How does Sasha's life compare to Becky's?**
The two identities represent opposite extremes of the protagonist's existence:

*   **Becky’s life** is characterized by loneliness and stagnation. Described as a "lonely twentysomething," her genuine life is mundane and lacks excitement.
*   **Sasha’s life** is an engineered fantasy. Through this persona, Becky gains access to a "close-knit" group of friends, secures a high-level job outside her actual experience through networking, and enters into a romantic affair with a widowed man (Elliot).

Ultimately, the text states that as Sasha, Becky leads a life that is **"far more exciting"** than her authentic life as Becky.

The term **big-endian** (and its counterpart, little-endian) was introduced to computer science by **Danny Cohen** in a 1980 Internet Experiment Note.

Cohen derived the terminology from the 1726 novel ***Gulliver's Travels*** by Jonathan Swift. In the book, the inhabitants of Lilliput are divided by a bitter conflict over the "correct" way to crack open a boiled egg: some break it from the big end, while others break it from the little end. Those who insisted on using the big end were referred to as "Big-Endians."

Cohen used this literary analogy to describe the order in which bytes are stored in memory: "big-endian" refers to systems that store the most significant byte at the lowest memory address, while "little-endian" refers to those that store the least significant byte first.

In business theory, disruptive innovation is innovation that creates a new market and value network or enters at the bottom of an existing market and eventually displaces established market-leading firms, products, and alliances. The concept was developed by the American academic Clayton Christensen and his collaborators beginning in 1995,[full citation needed] and has been called the most influential business idea of the early 21st century. Lingfei Wu, Dashun Wang, and James A. Evans generalized this term to identify disruptive science and technological advances from more than 65 million papers, patents and software products that span the period 1954–2014. Their work was featured as the cover of the February 2019 issue of Nature and was included among the Altmetric 100 most-discussed work in 2019. Not all innovations are disruptive, even if they are revolutionary. For example, the first automobiles in the late 19th century were not a disruptive innovation, because early automobiles were expensive luxury items that did not disrupt the market for horse-drawn vehicles. The market for transportation essentially remained intact until the debut of the lower-priced Ford Model T in 1908. The mass-produced automobile was a disruptive innovation, because it changed the transportation market, whereas the first thirty years of automobiles did not. The United States Military Academy is called West Point because it is on the western point of an S-turn on the Hudson River. During the American Revolution, the Revolutionary Army stretched an iron chain across the Hudson at this point because British ships would have to slow down to navigate the S-turn, making them susceptible to cannon fire. The British never tested the chain, and their Naval forces remained separated in Canada and New York. Most RVs also have generators, but generators are noisy and require either gas or diesel to run. Some RVs with lithium batteries (or more rarely, lead acid), have a second alternator installed that charges the batteries while driving. Finally, solar power is a popular option. **Pros (Advantages of Rational-Legal Authority)**
*   **Increased Efficiency:** By utilizing a rigid division of labor and regular execution of tasks, the organization can handle complex administrative duties more rationally and efficiently.
*   **Fairness and Equality:** Because qualifications are evaluated by organizational rules rather than individuals, the system promotes equal treatment and reduces personal bias in hiring and promotion.
*   **Expertise-Driven Results:** Requiring officials to have expert training and technical qualifications ensures that tasks are handled by competent professionals rather than amateurs.
*   **Clear Accountability:** The use of a hierarchical organization and formal lines of authority (chain of command) ensures that every member knows who they report to and who is responsible for specific decisions.
*   **Consistency and Predictability:** Since all powers and decisions are specified and restricted by regulations, the organization operates with a high level of stability and standardization.

**Cons (Disadvantages of the "Iron Cage")**
*   **Loss of Individual Freedom:** The strict adherence to rule-based, rational control can threaten individual liberties and limit personal autonomy within the workplace.
*   **Lack of Flexibility:** Because activities are restricted to a "fixed area" and governed by rigid regulations, the organization may struggle to adapt to unique situations that fall outside the rules.
*   **Dehumanization:** The process of extreme rationalization can create a "soulless" environment

**Primary Origin**

**Path to English**

*   **The Settlement Theory:** It may have arrived in American English via the Dutch settlement of New Netherland in the early 1600s, possibly through the informal dialect variant ***koekie***.
*   **The Attestation Theory:** It is formally attested in American English by 1808 in the sense of a "small, flat, sweet cake."

**Note on Scottish Usage**

During the American Revolution, the Revolutionary Army stretched an iron chain across the Hudson at this point because British ships would have to slow down to navigate the S-turn, making them susceptible to cannon fire. The British never tested the chain, and their Naval forces remained separated in Canada and New York. The six genres Bauer focuses upon are novels, autobiography, history and politics, drama, poetry and natural sciences. She describes how to approach each genre as a reader, how to ask good questions of the author and how to formulate your own viewpoint of the topic. For each genre, when presenting the book list, she gives you a summary of each book, the best revision of the book to read and her initial impressions of the authors viewpoint. Bauer's book is not meant to be read from cover to cover, but to be a guide as you work through the reading list of each genre. ### 1. What was 1MDB?
**1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB)** was a strategic development company founded in 2009 by then-Prime Minister of Malaysia, **Najib Razak**. 

On paper, it was a sovereign wealth fund intended to drive economic growth in Malaysia by investing in energy, real estate, and infrastructure. Because it was backed by the government, it had an easy time borrowing billions of dollars from global banks (like Goldman Sachs) and foreign governments.

### 2. How the Scandal Worked (The Mechanics)
The scandal was essentially a massive "shell game." Instead of the money going into development projects, billions were diverted through a series of complex transactions:

*   **Fake Joint Ventures:** 1MDB entered into "joint ventures" with companies that were actually shell corporations controlled by the conspirators.
*   **Overpriced Assets:** Money was spent on assets at inflated prices, with the "extra" money being kicked back to private accounts.
*   **The "Laundering" Cycle:** To hide the origin of the stolen money, it was moved through banks in Switzerland, Singapore, and Luxembourg before landing in private accounts or being spent on luxury items.

There are several reasons why JDAM is one of the most cost effective weapons ever invented. By using GPS navigation, the JDAM guidance kit can be extremely cheap, as low as $25k/kit. It is likely cheaper than any other precision-guided weapons. GPS navigation provides good targeting precision, typically within meters. Combined with blast radius of 500-2000 lbs unguided bombs, JDAM can effectively destroy any targets on the ground. Because JDAM has navigation capability, pilots no longer need to precisely aim the bombers against the targets. It allows a bomber to quickly and precisely hit multiple targets along the route. Some JDAM guidance kits include targeting sensors, such as laser targeting. They can be used against mobile targets, which further increases the use cases for JDAM. In summary, by combining dumb bombs with a guidance kit, JDAM becomes a very cost effective weapon system, and is widely adopted by the US and other military forces. Robert Metcalfe's primary impact on society was the invention and standardization of **Ethernet**.

His contributions shaped modern connectivity in the following ways:

*   **Creation of Local Area Networks (LANs):** While working at Xerox PARC in 1973, Metcalfe (along with David Boggs) developed Ethernet as a standard for connecting computers over short distances. This allowed computers to communicate efficiently via "packets of data."
*   **Establishing a Dominant Industry Standard:** Through the co-founding of 3Com, a manufacturer of networking equipment, Metcalfe helped Ethernet become the dominant networking standard for local area networks.
*   **Advancement of Network Theory:** By identifying and fixing bugs in the AlohaNet model for his doctoral thesis, he contributed to the technical foundation of how data is transmitted and handled (including managing collisions and retransmissions) in networking.
*   **Education and Innovation:** In his later career, he influenced future technologists as a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, focusing on innovation initiatives, and as a research affiliate at MIT.

Tzatziki is a traditional Greek sauce whose base ingredients comprise salted strained yoghurt, garlic, grated cucumber, dill leaves, and olive oil. To make your tzatziki truly exceptional follow the steps below: 1) Start by squeezing as much as possible the water out of half a cucumber that has been grated. This is the single most important factor that will make your tzatziki source exceptional. 2) Fine-chop the dill leaves using a knife. The dill must be fresh. The volume of the chopped dill leaves should be about the same as the volume of the squeezed grated cucumber. 3) Mix the cucumber and the dill with Greek strained yoghurt . The latter should have a volume that is three to four times that of the cucumber and dill. 4) Add some salt and smashed cloves of fresh garlic. 5) Add a couple of teaspoons of balsamic vinegar. 6) While stirring the mix, gradually keep adding extra virgin olive oil until the sauce obtains a silky texture. 7) Do not add any other ingredients in the mix. 8) Place the mix in the fridge and keep it for a couple of hours and let chemistry do its magic. 9) Remove the residual water, if any, which may have surfaced. 10) Stir the mix once more final time and serve in smaller containers.
